facts.claim: "WMP" is track 1 on Medium Build's 9-track album roughboy, released November 21, 2018, and runs 3:16.
All songs on roughboy, including "WMP", were written by Nicholas Carpenter and James Glaves.
roughboy was mixed and mastered by James Glaves.
The roughboy lineup was Nick Carpenter (vocals, guitar) with James Glaves (guitar/keyboards), James Dommek Jr. (drums) and Chad Reynvaan (bass).
Glaves said almost every roughboy track was written about a specific real-life situation that he or Carpenter lived through, including love lost, anxiety, depression, suicide and addiction.
Anchorage Daily News described roughboy as having a distinct '80s feel, richly layered without feeling overproduced, with candid lyricism. It came about six months after the album softboy.
Medium Build's discography runs Falling Apart (2016), then softboy and roughboy (both 2018), then Wild (2019).
Medium Build is the project of Nick Carpenter, who studied music at Middle Tennessee State, dropped out, and moved to Anchorage, Alaska. His brother had lived there since 2009.
Carpenter met producer James Glaves at an Anchorage open mic. Glaves then joined as co-writer and producer for about three years.
Carpenter has said the Medium Build name began as a joke and served as a safe place to hide and fail.

research.lineage: Anchorage, Alaska-scene indie/alternative pop with an '80s synth-pop feel and blunt, confessional singer-songwriter lyrics.

draft:
The most damning line in **WMP** is also the gentlest: "Babe, I'll be in bed in just a minute." It follows the admission that the narrator's face is glued to his phone, and it lands like every promise made half-turned away from the person waiting. Nick Carpenter sings it in a clear, slightly nasal voice, set up front in a clean, dry mix. He sounds like he's telling you across a kitchen table, not from a stage.

The song is a ledger of advice and accusations. It opens on the life advice handed down to him, "Be a good hang, a decent guy," a creed so low-bar it reads as a joke and a trap at once. Then come the nights: blackouts, a "whole new me" who grabs the wheel and drives home drunk. The woman he's sleeping with says he's too much like her dad, too in love with his own head, a product of white male privilege. The title's initials come from her verdict, not his. He doesn't argue. He reports it as flatly as he reports the drinking, then retreats into a chorus that shrugs: too late to work out where he went wrong, so he'll be alone. Self-pity and self-indictment share the same breath, and the song won't choose between them.

The arrangement keeps all of that small. An acoustic guitar picks out a simple arpeggiated figure, bass holds root notes, drums keep a plain beat, and the groove has a steady, melancholy sway. A second voice shadows the lead, so the confession sounds less like a soliloquy and more like two people admitting the same thing. Carpenter wrote it with James Glaves, who also mixed and mastered roughboy. Glaves has said nearly every song on the record came from something one of them actually lived through, from lost love to addiction.

Then the bridge breaks open. Told to make plans, and afraid of messing them up again, he recites the script: buy a house, have kids, get a job, "Hang rope lights in the backyard," then a minivan, then a second house on the lake. Each item is more ordinary than the last. The promise that everything will be fine curdles into a repeated "oh my god" that stretches until it's nearly a howl. It's hard to tell whether he's reaching for that life or choking on it. Probably both.

Carpenter started Medium Build after leaving music school in Tennessee for Anchorage, and he's called the name a safe place to hide and fail. As the opening track on roughboy, this song sets that terms sheet out plainly: the failures, lined up in order, with no excuses attached.

You end up holding both halves of him at once, the man who knows exactly what's wrong with himself and the one still promising, from the next room, that he'll be right there.
